newsitem.title: UK: London to survive DMG storm but rules under review.
newsitem.headline: London to survive DMG storm but rules under review.

text.p: London's flourishing fund management industry will survive the Morgan Grenfell furore but calls for more regulation at the retail end of the market are likely, industry sources said on Friday.

Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), part of the Deutsche Bank group, was forced to suspend three European funds worth 1.4 billion stg ($2.19 billion) this week. Their managers were suspended pending investigations.

The funds resumed trading on Thursday after a 180 million stg bailout by Deutsche Bank but investors immediately sold over eight percent of the three funds as a murky saga of ties with unlisted private Luxembourg companies unfolded.
The focus of concern was that the funds targetted ordinary investors, some 90,000 of whom entrusted their savings to a manager with an apparantly solid gold reputation.

"Because it involved unit trusts -- the retail end of the market -- there is bound to be some justifiable pressure to tighten regulations at the margin," said Michael Cassidy, Chairman of Policy and Resources at the Corporation of London.

"We would invite IMRO (the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation) and SIB (the Securities and Investments Board) to see if there are some minor changes to the regulations here that will deal with the loophole."
But London's position as the world's fund management centre would not be jeopardised.
City directors said London would retain its edge, certainly over other European centres, because of its "critical mass" of both expertise and volume of business, and its liquid labour market.
Last year London overtook New York as the world's biggest centre for fund management activity. It had some 987 billion stg in the business in 1995 -- already up to one trillion stg now.

The UK unit trust association, AUTIF, has defended the industry, saying tight regulation ensured that the fund manager's unusual activity was detected in the first place. "The reputation of the industry is jealously guarded; no unit trust investor here has ever lost any money as a result of irregularities," said AUTIF dirtector Philip Warland. London's reputation has been helped by Morgan Grenfell and Deutsche Bank stepping in with full compensation.
But Deutsche Bank board member Rolf Breuer has indicated the bank is considering relocating the business to Frankfurt.
"I am not criticising the regulatory authorities, but it could not have happened in Germany," he told the Financial Times. "Valuations are the responsibility of the custodian."

Other unit trust industry sources said fund managers would urge UK regulators to review limits on fund holdings of pure unlisted stock, of prelisted or "approved" stock about to be brought to market and of checking procedures.

Fiona Munro at the Association of Investment Trust Companies, closed-end funds that also attract some retail involvement, said their independent boards controlled the funds. There were no limits on holdings of unlisted stock, but the board had ultimate responsibility for fair valuation.
"IMRO perhaps needs to look at the rules on holding unlisted companies and I am sure they are doing that," she added.
Corporation of London's Cassidy said he would be watching carefullly to see whether Deutsche Bank moved control of its unit trust operation to Frankfurt, or the actual operation.

He was "reasonably relaxed" about the idea of management control from Frankfurt. "But we would be concerned about moving the actual operation, although obviously they have to do everything necessary to restore confidence."
London should not jeopardise its balanced attitude to investment regulation because of the incident, he added.

"We don't want to be cowboy country...but you have to be careful not to be too heavy-handed otherwise it all goes offshore and then you really can't do anything about it. There is always another centre that will take your business if you regulate too hard."
